doc.title: Hal Espinosa interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, March 20, 2024

title: Virtual orchestra grievance and arbitration with the Nederlanders
summary: As Local 47 president, Hal fought a virtual orchestra that replaced six pit musicians and settled with Jimmy Nederlander, then mentions tape's effect.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: How the music business changed: hype, youth and lost apprenticeship

blocks.x: The virtual orchestra. Thank you. That’s the problem I had when I was president of the local. We had in our contracts with the theaters there a minimum of at least 18 musicians. New York — their minimums usually were like 24 for their largest theaters. And our theaters that we have in L.A. they were all larger than the largest one other than where the Rockettes perform. You know that’s a big one. But at that time they were all maybe 1000 seats, 800 seats, 1200 maybe. Ours were like 1800 seats and similar to that, 1600 I think at the — one of them up in Beverly Hills. Anyway that’s — instead of our minimum at 24, we had ours at 18 so that’s what I inherited when I became president was 18. And they were trying to downsize the road musicians. So when it got to L.A. they wanted to have some of their musicians be put in the pit and eliminate some of our people like the drummer would be out, maybe the concertmaster, and that would be it. The others would have to go on vacation for three weeks or four weeks, at least two weeks because no show came to L.A. for less than a couple of weeks anyway. So even the old shows that came in they were there at least for two weeks. And there were times when I got to know the Neiderlanders — Jimmy Neiderlander, who owned you know half of Broadway at the time. I got to meet him. And one time they brought in a virtual orchestra. And replaced six of our musicians. So we had in our contract no virtual orchestra and 18 minimum. So we filed a grievance against them and we were going to go to arbitration. So we took them to arbitration. They brought over an attorney that was costing I figured around $500 an hour, this was in 2002. He flew out — he was from Washington, D.C. He flew out, stayed at the Peninsula Hotel in Beverly Hills, it started at $400 a night. And so Jimmy called me up after we had one arbitration hearing. Jimmy called me and he says, “Hal, why are you suing me?” Jimmy was like, had to be 70 at least then. I said, “Jimmy, we aren’t suing you,” I said, “Your people here in L.A. broke our agreement that we both signed. They brought in this virtual orchestra to replace six musicians.” He said, “Well that’s how the show operates, you know it comes in with that.” I said, “Well then you’ve got to check the agreement and you need to call us and let us know, or tell them they can’t come in with that virtual orchestra because we’ve got a minimum of musicians.” So he says, “Well you know this is costing me $50,000 already.” I said, “For the arbitration?” I said, “Jimmy,” I said, “I know it’s expensive, your attorney must cost you

$500 an hour.” He said, “$600.” So I was close. And then I said — he brought an assistant with him who had to be maybe $300 and they’re staying at The Peninsula, I said it’s cost — so you’re paying his first class air, staying at the most expensive place in L.A., and I said, “The arbitration, we’ve only started this, we’ve got the two guys in New York who invented the virtual orchestra coming out, you know, for the hearing and the arbitration.” And then we had Bill Moriarity, who was the president of New York at that time. We flew him out to be a witness about New York’s contracts and how they can’t be in there and why they shouldn’t be in L.A. So anyway Jimmy said, “What can we do?” He said, “I don’t want to spend any more money, what can we do to make this go away?” So I thought for a minute and I said, “Jimmy” there were six musicians that we had to cancel that were replaced on the first show and then the second show that came in two weeks later for two weeks, replaced six musicians. So I said, “If you paid their wages then maybe we can make this go away.” But I said, “I’m going to have to talk to the musicians first to see if they’re okay with that.” So he said, “I’ll get right back to you.” No then he said, “How much do you think this is going to cost?” I said, thinking, “probably around $30,000.” So he said, “Let me get back to you.” So 15 minutes later I got this henchman on the phone saying, “Hal” and I knew him, he said, “Jimmy wants to make a deal. He’ll pay six musicians for both shows.” So I said, “Well it’s not a done deal yet because I’ve got to have a meeting with the orchestra and see if they’re okay with that.” So they were. You know they took the money. But those are the kinds of things I dealt with with the theater pit. But prior to that when I was still playing the trumpet, you know back when I was a kid I went to see the Red Skelton Show at CBS and this is back in the early ‘50s when somebody screwed up on stage they had to stop and start all over again because they didn’t have tape. Musicians, if they screwed up you heard the cracked note or a squeak or whatever it might have been at that time because they didn’t have tape. I don’t believe it was until maybe in the ‘60s when they got the tape because at that time we, you know we were working a whole lot more being rehearsal pianists for shows or dancers, you know performing, getting ready for a TV show or a movie. They made money. Then pretty soon after the tape, they’d record the musicians and the rhythm section and they’d just loop it and play it in rehearsals and cut musicians out. And they cut us out. So that was the beginning of new technology for us that we had to deal with. And in the theaters the main thing, motion pictures was another too because they started going down to smaller orchestras. And like New York would have maybe 10% of all the music that was done on union contracts. We did about 90% of all the musics that were done on union contracts. So we had the majority of them.
